brief.situation: 10:00 on a medical unit. You are the RN on the unit's practice council. Your manager Marta wants you to start a 'quality project' tomorrow: randomize patients to two mouth-care routines, collect their names, record numbers and pneumonia outcomes in a spreadsheet, and write it up for a nursing journal. She says IRB review 'takes months' and a quality project doesn't need it. She hands you a journal article as the model. Work out what is being asked, act on your professional code and the research rules, and keep the working relationship where you can.
handover: Your professional code puts the patient first, including the rights of people who take part in research.

Hospital policy: anything that may be research, including quality projects designed to produce generalizable knowledge, goes to the IRB office for a determination before it starts; patient identifiers stay in approved systems.
howItWorks: Choose what to ask or say. Each exchange takes a few minutes of the conversation; Marta answers at once, and the next choice waits for the exchange to finish.
The screen shows Marta, how hard she is pushing, your working relationship, what you know so far, and your note.
When the conversation ends you write your note and explain your reasoning.

reflection.question: For your note: what the ethical problem was, what you did about it and why, and how you dealt with your manager.

parts.label: The problem
parts.criteria: Names that randomizing patients and publishing to produce generalizable knowledge is likely research needing an IRB determination and consent rules, that identifiers on a shared drive breach privacy, and that an article with no consent or IRB statement is a warning sign.
parts.modelAnswer: Randomizing patients and publishing for other hospitals is research, not just QI, so it needs an IRB decision and consent rules. Names on a shared drive is a privacy problem, and the model article never mentions consent or IRB, which is a red flag.

parts.label: Ask, then act
parts.criteria: Asks what the project does and is for, and checks the model article and whether anyone asked the IRB, before answering; declines and offers a route that meets the goal (a determination this week and a non-identifying practice audit now).
parts.modelAnswer: I asked what it was for and checked the article and the IRB question, then said not as planned and offered a determination this week plus an audit we can start now.

parts.label: The relationship and the channel
parts.criteria: Acknowledges the goal; brings in the IRB office and nurse researcher, not threats or a public post; writes a factual note.
parts.modelAnswer: I agreed the goal matters, brought in the IRB office and the nurse researcher, and wrote it down.

costly.headline: Protected, at a cost
costly.body: The criteria show the cost: a late answer, a refusal with no way forward, a threat or a public post, or a relationship worse than it needed to be.

breached.headline: Human subjects unprotected

scoring.modelReasoning: Quality improvement becomes research when it is designed to contribute to generalizable knowledge; the intent to publish alone does not decide it, but randomizing patients and writing it up for other hospitals does point to research, which needs an IRB determination and consent unless the IRB waives it. An article that never mentions consent or IRB approval is a warning sign. Acknowledge the goal, decline the plan as written, offer a determination this week and a non-identifying practice audit now, keep identifiers in approved systems, bring in the IRB office and nurse researcher, and write a factual note.
